scope: Research summaries across the existing collection and November additions from Nature Portfolio, NeurIPS, ICML and ICLR. Paper dates, manuscript revisions and website addition dates are shown separately.

prediction.description: From human activity recognition to health modeling: body signals, digital measures and models for monitoring health and predicting disease risk.

evolution.headline: Build shared recordings for testing models
evolution.change: Annotated heart-signal datasets give researchers common examples and labels to test against.
evolution.meaning: This supplies the data needed for later learning methods; it is not itself a reusable AI model.
evolution.limit: This stage covers shared data resources collected before 2021.

evolution.headline: Reuse what a model learns across datasets
evolution.change: BENDR learns patterns from unlabelled brain recordings. BIOT extends cross-dataset learning to different body signals.
evolution.meaning: A trained model becomes a reusable component alongside the shared recordings.
evolution.limit: Transfer to another dataset still needs testing.

evolution.headline: Learn from several signals together
evolution.change: SleepFM combines brain, heart and breathing recordings to learn reusable patterns for sleep-related tasks.
evolution.meaning: Compared with the earlier transfer examples, this study tests how several simultaneous signals can contribute to one model.
evolution.limit: The study uses sleep-lab recordings. Its results do not establish performance on everyday smartwatch data.

evolution.headline: Connect sensor readings with language
evolution.change: SensorLM links sensor sequences to text. PH-LLM studies personalised reasoning about longer wearable histories.
evolution.meaning: Alongside signal analysis, the target now includes describing and reasoning about a person's data in words.
evolution.limit: A fluent answer can still be wrong. These are research tasks, not proof of safe medical advice.

evolution.headline: Learn across sensors and test transfer to new settings
evolution.change: xMAE builds physiological timing into training. EEG-X handles changing EEG layouts, and EmoPhone tests transfer across people and collection waves.
evolution.meaning: Reusable models need tests that reflect changes in the sensor, user and recording conditions.
evolution.limit: Reported gains use different tasks and metrics; each comparison is reported with its own setup.

prediction.headline: Models learn across body signals; new benchmarks test where they transfer
prediction.summary: xMAE uses the timing between ECG and PPG. BioX-Bridge transfers knowledge between signal types, and EEG-X reuses models across headsets. New benchmarks test longer recordings and changes between study populations. The common question is whether a reusable model still works when the task, person or sensor changes.
prediction.status: Our comparison of the cited model and benchmark studies
prediction.use: For health-data teams: compare the signals available, the test population and the adaptation cost. The consumer-API study is a useful check on what heart rate and step counts can predict.
prediction.takeaway: EEG-X reports a 1.67-percentage-point gain in one cross-device test. xMAE improves 15 of 19 tested tasks. EmoPhone adds repeated collection waves for testing changes over time.

dimensions.answer: Use the relationship between sensors during training
dimensions.text: xMAE preserves ECG-PPG timing. BioX-Bridge connects models trained on different signals with a small trainable bridge.

dimensions.answer: Test across people and collection years
dimensions.text: EmoPhone contains 282 people and 53,139 momentary self-reports. Inertia-1 compares design choices using over 18.2 million hours of movement recordings.

dimensions.answer: Adapt the software to different headsets and small processors
dimensions.text: EEG-X covers five EEG headset configurations. HiMAE evaluates running a multi-resolution signal model on smartwatch-class CPUs.

dimensions.answer: Ask questions about signals and find events using text
dimensions.text: SleepLM adds descriptions, retrieval and language-guided event localization. HEARTS tests which health-signal reasoning tasks language models can handle.

dimensions.answer: Compare gains within the same task and test setup
dimensions.text: EEG-X scores 37.58% versus 35.91% balanced accuracy in one frozen-encoder transfer test. BioX-Bridge reduces trainable parameters by 88% to 99% in its tested adaptations.

dimensions.answer: Check the information available through real device APIs
dimensions.text: In a 16-person study, models using Fitbit heart rate and steps had mean AUROC between 0.569 and 0.617 for substance use or craving. The choice of accessible signal affects the task.

stories.name: EEG-X
stories.headline: Reuse a brain-signal model across different headsets
stories.change: Channel locations and reconstruction of cleaned activity help the encoder transfer across sensor layouts.
stories.result: Across eight datasets and five headset configurations, one TUAB-to-BCICIV_2A test reached 37.58% balanced accuracy, compared with REVE's 35.91%.
stories.before: Changing electrode layouts makes it difficult to reuse an EEG encoder across headsets.
stories.benefit: Teams can evaluate a shared encoder across different headset layouts.
stories.condition: This comparison freezes the pretrained encoder and trains a linear classifier under the paper's transfer protocol.
stories.locator: Latest manuscript, Table 3: TUAB-to-BCICIV_2A linear evaluation

stories.name: EmoPhone
stories.headline: Test affect sensing across people and annual collection waves
stories.change: Android and Fitbit recordings cover three annual waves, with tests across people, time and collection waves.
stories.result: The dataset includes 282 people, 297 participant-wave records and 53,139 momentary self-reports. Fourteen people returned in later waves.
stories.before: A single collection period gives little evidence about transfer across different annual study waves.
stories.benefit: Benchmark across changing users and collection conditions before choosing a sensing model for daily use.
stories.condition: In the latest full paper, adaptation improves its MLP backbone while supervised tree models remain competitive.
stories.locator: November v2 full paper: dataset and cross-wave results

stories.name: xMAE
stories.headline: Teach a model how heart and pulse signals are related
stories.change: Masked reconstruction across ECG and PPG teaches a model to preserve the delay between heart electrical activity and the peripheral pulse.
stories.result: The paper reports stronger performance than unimodal and multimodal baselines on 15 of 19 downstream tasks.
stories.before: Pretraining often treats ECG and PPG as interchangeable views, losing their physiological timing relationship.
stories.benefit: Known relationships between sensors can guide pretraining and improve transfer across devices.
stories.condition: The 19 tasks include cardiovascular outcomes, laboratory results, sleep stages and demographic attributes.
stories.locator: Formal proceedings abstract and cross-modal reconstruction method

prediction.latest_summary: EEG-X tests transfer across headsets. EmoPhone adds multiple years of real-life sensing data. ICML and ICLR papers add cross-signal learning and health-reasoning tests.

intervention.description: Use wearable data and health records to compare possible actions, design adaptive support and test treatment effects.

evolution.headline: Work out how to compare treatment choices
evolution.change: Marginal structural models address changing treatment and patient history. Later repeated-randomisation trial designs test when support helps.
evolution.meaning: Define the action and estimate its effect on the outcome of interest.
evolution.limit: Estimating an effect from existing records requires assumptions; a randomised trial answers a different kind of evidence question.

evolution.headline: Study the timing and sequence of actions
evolution.change: HeartSteps tests walking suggestions at repeated moments. Causal Transformer estimates outcomes under changing treatment sequences.
evolution.meaning: Compared with a single treatment choice, these examples ask when to act and how earlier decisions affect later outcomes.
evolution.limit: A model's estimated treatment response is not the same as benefit demonstrated in a trial.

evolution.headline: Use richer sensor outcomes and responsive devices
evolution.change: ADD MALTS compares patterns of wearable measurements. InTandem adjusts musical cues to a person's walking.
evolution.meaning: Methods can retain more of the sensor record, while devices can change their output as movement changes.
evolution.limit: The method and treatment studies use separate tasks and evaluation designs.

evolution.headline: Check whether tailored advice improves health
evolution.change: myBPmyLife tests activity and food suggestions in 602 adults with hypertension. It did not improve the main blood-pressure outcome compared with control.
evolution.meaning: The main blood-pressure outcome remained similar between groups while some behaviours improved.
evolution.limit: This result concerns this intervention and population, not every adaptive health system.

evolution.headline: Add personal-data reasoning and more detailed movement feedback
evolution.change: The Personal Health Agent coordinates analysis and coaching. EEG experiments detect movement mismatch during virtual and electrically stimulated actions.
evolution.meaning: These functions help a system interpret needs and detect errors; outcome trials assess the effects of using the resulting support.
evolution.limit: The assistant uses expert and user ratings; movement-error classification was tested in able-bodied volunteers.

intervention.headline: Wearable records guide health conversations and movement feedback
intervention.summary: The Personal Health Agent combines data analysis with coaching. A separate EEG experiment detects when intended and stimulated arm movements differ. These studies add ways to interpret personal records and measure feedback. The existing trials show which advice and treatment packages changed health outcomes.
intervention.status: Our comparison of assistant evaluations, feedback experiments and trials
intervention.use: For coaching and rehabilitation teams: decide what the system must change, then measure that outcome. Conversation ratings, movement-error detection and treatment response answer different design questions.
intervention.takeaway: New work improves the quality of health conversations and supplies a candidate feedback signal for stimulation. Existing outcome trials remain the basis for judging treatment benefit.

dimensions.answer: Coordinate analysis, health knowledge and coaching
dimensions.text: The Personal Health Agent assigns parts of a question to specialist agents and combines their responses.

dimensions.answer: Bring wearable histories into the health conversation
dimensions.text: The assistant uses wearable histories, laboratory results and conversation context. Experts and users evaluate its replies.

dimensions.answer: Combine EEG with virtual movement and electrical stimulation
dimensions.text: The movement study records EEG while participants compare intended movements with an avatar or stimulation of their own arm.

dimensions.answer: Detect a mismatch that could guide the next action
dimensions.text: Error-related brain activity supplies feedback when a movement differs from its target.

dimensions.answer: Measure the specific function being added
dimensions.text: PHA's expert conversation-quality score is 72.8%, versus 54.4% for PHIA. The EEG study reports 91 ± 13% classification accuracy at its best tested feature window for large movement mismatches.

dimensions.answer: Connect feedback to decisions, then test the resulting support
dimensions.text: The new studies evaluate conversation quality and error detection. Existing randomized trials provide separate evidence about the health outcomes of a delivered intervention.

stories.name: Personal Health Agent
stories.headline: A health assistant combines calculations with personal coaching
stories.change: A coordinator brings together wearable-data analysis, health knowledge and personal coaching.
stories.result: Experts rated overall conversation quality at 72.8%, compared with 54.4% for PHIA and 64.3% for parallel agents.
stories.before: Single-agent PHIA or parallel specialists answer using the same Gemini backbone.
stories.benefit: Personal health assistants can connect calculations with advice, with response quality and latency assessed together.
stories.condition: The live study used 45 people role-playing 50 health-data personas; the outcome was conversation quality.

stories.name: EEG movement-error feedback
stories.headline: Brain signals identify when an assisted movement misses its target
stories.change: EEG measures responses to mismatches between intended arm movements and an avatar or electrically stimulated movement.
stories.result: Five volunteers completed discrete-movement tests and 16 completed continuous-movement tests. At the best tested feature window, electrical-stimulation classification accuracy averaged 91 ± 13%.
stories.before: A stimulation controller needs feedback about whether its movement matches the person's intended movement.
stories.benefit: Detected movement errors provide a signal that future stimulation controllers could use for feedback.
stories.condition: Participants were able-bodied. Continuous-movement classifiers used large mismatches and unequal error/no-error trial counts.

stories.name: Pace Me trial
stories.headline: Activity-triggered messages did not improve the main outcome
stories.change: The app adds a wearable tracker and messages at set activity levels to support energy management.
stories.result: The six-month trial randomised 250 people. It found no better main result for symptoms after exertion than the comparison group.
stories.before: The comparison app provided data-entry screens rather than the tracker-linked support package.
stories.benefit: Helps teams assess the added value of a tracker-linked support package.
stories.condition: The six-month Long COVID trial randomized 250 people; its final per-protocol analysis included 161.
stories.locator: Abstract: design, participant counts and primary outcome

intervention.latest_summary: A Nature health assistant coordinates analysis and coaching. A November EEG study detects errors during avatar and electrically stimulated arm movements.

twin.description: Models of an individual's changing physiology, updated with personal data to simulate possible trajectories and treatment choices.

evolution.headline: Test a personal model inside insulin treatment
evolution.change: A trial tests digital-twin-supported experimentation as part of automated insulin delivery.
evolution.meaning: The trial evaluates the personal model within a treatment system.
evolution.limit: The trial evaluates a diabetes-specific treatment package.

evolution.headline: Check forecast errors and update the personal model
evolution.change: The ICU glucose study tests error-triggered adaptation with 15- and 30-minute forecasts. Another diabetes study uses weekly retraining and daily feedback.
evolution.meaning: A personal model can be designed around a measurable update loop, with a defined task and time horizon.
evolution.limit: The ICU study is retrospective and evaluates forecasting; the daily-feedback study is a separate small trial.

twin.headline: Personal models update their predictions as new measurements arrive
twin.summary: The new ICU glucose study tests a concrete update loop: predict, check the next measurements and adapt when errors grow. Earlier diabetes studies connect personal models to treatment adjustment or daily feedback. The engineering choices are what the model represents, how it updates and which decision it informs.
twin.status: Our comparison of individual glucose models and treatment frameworks
twin.use: For teams building personal models: specify the measurements, prediction horizon and update rule. Keep forecast evaluation and treatment evaluation distinct in the development plan.
twin.takeaway: The October study adapts a pretrained model to ten ICU patients in seconds on a laptop, then tests rolling 15- and 30-minute glucose forecasts.

dimensions.answer: Update the model when new readings show growing errors
dimensions.text: The ICU study uses a pretrained PatchTST model and checks its forecasts against incoming glucose measurements.

dimensions.answer: Use repeated measurements from the person being modelled
dimensions.text: The new study evaluates ten septic ICU patients after pretraining on one patient's glucose data.

dimensions.answer: Run adaptation on a laptop using continuous glucose records
dimensions.text: The contribution is the model-update workflow and its computation time. The study uses inpatient CGM recordings.

dimensions.answer: Forecast the next 15 or 30 minutes of glucose
dimensions.text: The model uses the latest 30 minutes of measurements. Earlier diabetes work uses model updates to support daily feedback.

dimensions.answer: Measure adaptation time and patient-specific forecast error
dimensions.text: Personalization takes seconds on a standard laptop. The retrospective tests compare ways to adapt predictions to each patient.

dimensions.answer: Connect individual prediction with decisions about support
dimensions.text: The ICU workflow checks forecasts continuously. Earlier insulin-care and feedback studies evaluate other ways to use personal models.

stories.name: Adaptive ICU glucose twin
stories.date: 2026-10-01 published · npj Metabolic Health and Disease
stories.headline: A personal glucose model checks and updates its forecasts
stories.change: A pretrained PatchTST model checks new glucose readings and adapts when forecast errors require an update.
stories.result: Ten septic ICU patients were evaluated after pretraining on one patient's data. Thirty minutes of readings supported 15- or 30-minute forecasts; personalization took seconds on a laptop.
stories.before: A fixed model forecasts without checking when an individual's signal patterns have changed.
stories.benefit: A personal model needs a defined update rule, a prediction horizon and a way to check its errors.
stories.condition: The retrospective study tested inpatient glucose forecasts; dosing decisions remained outside the evaluated workflow.
stories.locator: Digital twin workflow; methods for the ten additional ICU patients

stories.name: Type 2 diabetes predictive twin
stories.headline: Weekly model updates support daily personal feedback
stories.change: Personal models are retrained weekly and generate daily text-message suggestions, with nurse-scored safeguards.
stories.result: Nineteen people were analysed: 10 in the AI group and 9 in the comparison group. Weight outcomes differed; glucose remained stable.
stories.before: The comparison uses self-monitoring and periodic care without model-generated daily feedback.
stories.benefit: Shows one way to connect a personal model with support between visits.
stories.condition: Single-centre analysis of 19 participants, with nurse-scored safeguards. Glucose remained stable during the study.
stories.locator: Methods: participant selection and model updates; results

stories.name: Twin-supported insulin-delivery trial
stories.headline: Test the personal model inside a treatment system
stories.change: Individual glucose-insulin models support treatment adjustment as part of a larger care package.
stories.result: The repository’s source review reports 72 participants over six months and improved time in the target glucose range for the full package.
stories.before: The study compares twin-guided adjustment with conventional feedback around automated insulin delivery.
stories.benefit: An earlier trial of treatment decisions supported by a personal model.
stories.condition: Six-month, 72-participant diabetes trial of the full twin-supported treatment package.
stories.verification: Existing source review retained; original page could not be reopened in this check

twin.latest_summary: An October glucose study tests rapid patient adaptation and error-triggered updates. Its data come from ICU monitoring; earlier work covers personal diabetes feedback and insulin care.

interface.description: Wearable sensing, body input and mixed reality as potential ways to display and interact with a personal digital twin.

evolution.headline: Build datasets for brain and muscle controls
evolution.change: Motor-imagery and hand-movement datasets support testing interfaces driven by brain or muscle recordings. MOABB makes brain-interface comparisons more consistent.
evolution.meaning: These resources make controlled comparisons possible before claiming that an interface works across users.
evolution.limit: The work supplies recordings and a benchmark for testing sensing models.

evolution.headline: Include what the wearer sees in daily life
evolution.change: Ego4D provides videos recorded from the wearer's viewpoint during everyday activities.
evolution.meaning: Alongside body-signal controls, researchers can study actions in their visual surroundings.
evolution.limit: This branch studies body input through a different sensing approach.

evolution.headline: Link viewpoints and record detailed hand actions
evolution.change: Ego-Exo4D pairs wearer and outside views. emg2pose and emg2qwerty provide wrist-muscle data for hand pose and typing.
evolution.meaning: The data support more detailed questions than which broad activity or gesture occurred.
evolution.limit: The dataset supports testing first-person context and interactions under the study's recording conditions.

evolution.headline: Train muscle controls across people and tasks
evolution.change: The generic neuromotor-interface study trains a noninvasive muscle-signal model across users and interaction tasks.
evolution.meaning: Compared with collecting labelled movements, the focus is now how widely one control model can be reused.
evolution.limit: Performance still depends on the task, device and user conditions that were tested.

evolution.headline: Improve long-term input and integrate touch with wearable displays
evolution.change: Dry electrodes support multiday muscle-signal control. Magnetic sensing tracks muscle movement, and pixel fibres combine touch sensing with a garment display.
evolution.meaning: Input stability and usable output surfaces are practical design targets alongside richer software.
evolution.limit: These studies evaluate research prototypes; their tasks and sensors differ.

interface.headline: More stable body input and touch displays expand wearable interaction
interface.summary: New electrodes keep muscle-signal decoding stable for days. Magnetic beads let an external sensor measure muscle movement directly. Pixel fibres turn a garment sleeve into a touch-sensitive display. These studies address different parts of an interface: acquiring signals, controlling a device and showing information.
interface.status: Our comparison of sensing and interaction prototypes
interface.use: For wearable-interface teams: compare calibration effort, movement tracking and interaction tasks. Separate laboratory prototypes from products available to users.
interface.takeaway: The dry-electrode study maintains EMG control for 14 days without retraining. The textile prototype combines a 96 × 54-pixel display with touch input.

dimensions.answer: Improve signal stability at the body interface
dimensions.text: Carbon-nanotube dry electrodes reduce drift. Magnetic sensing measures muscle mechanics alongside the electrical activity used by EMG.

dimensions.answer: Test real control tasks over time
dimensions.text: The electrode study follows 14 days without decoder retraining. Three participants with amputations test magnetic control of a virtual ankle-foot cursor.

dimensions.answer: Add stable electrodes, magnetic tracking and textile displays
dimensions.text: The new work changes the sensing contact, the measured physical signal and the surface used for display and touch.

dimensions.answer: Use body signals for control and clothing for touch input
dimensions.text: Magnetic tracking drives a virtual prosthetic cursor. Pixel fibres support touch, video and wireless image transfer on a sleeve.

dimensions.answer: Read the measurement that matches the interface task
dimensions.text: EMG control remains stable for 14 days. The sleeve provides 96 × 54 pixels, 8-bit colour and 30 frames per second for video without audio.

dimensions.answer: Connect wearable sensing with displays that fit daily use
dimensions.text: The new prototypes cover stable input, body control and garment output. Smart-glasses software remains another route for presenting information.

stories.name: Multi-day EMG electrodes
stories.headline: Keep muscle-signal control stable without daily retraining
stories.change: Breathable carbon-nanotube dry electrodes maintain skin contact and reduce drift and movement artifacts.
stories.result: The multichannel EMG interface maintained task performance for 14 days without decoder retraining after minutes of initial training.
stories.before: Changes at the electrode-skin contact can force muscle-signal decoders to be recalibrated.
stories.benefit: Stable sensing hardware can reduce the calibration work required for long-term body-input systems.
stories.condition: The result concerns the tested electrophysiology interface and recording conditions.
stories.locator: Abstract and multiday EMG interface results

stories.name: Magnetic muscle sensing
stories.headline: Track muscle movement directly for virtual prosthetic control
stories.change: A skin-mounted array tracks 3-mm implanted magnetic beads to measure muscle movement directly.
stories.result: Three participants with below-knee amputations controlled a virtual ankle-foot cursor. The system tracked beads at depths up to 6 cm with sub-millimetre resolution.
stories.before: EMG interfaces infer movement from muscle electrical activity.
stories.benefit: Muscle mechanics offer another input alongside electrical signals for assistive-device control.
stories.condition: Participants controlled an on-screen cursor representing prosthetic movement; walking with a physical prosthesis was outside this experiment.

stories.name: Touch-sensitive textile display
stories.headline: A garment sleeve becomes a touch-sensitive display
stories.change: One fibre architecture combines individually addressable LEDs, connections and touch sensing in a garment sleeve.
stories.result: The prototype has 96 × 54 pixels, 8-bit colour and 30 frames per second, with touch input and wireless image transfer.
stories.before: Fibre displays separated display circuitry from touch localization.
stories.benefit: Clothing can display information and accept touch input at the same surface.
stories.condition: The 30-frame rate is for video without audio; synchronized audio-video was demonstrated at 25 frames per second.

interface.latest_summary: Nature-family papers add longer-lasting EMG input, magnetic muscle tracking and a touch-sensitive garment display. Each improves a different part of wearable interaction.
